title: The Supreme Court First Gave Students Constitutional Rights, Then Shrunk Them: From Flag Salutes to Backpack Searches
dek: From refusing to salute the flag to searching backpacks, six rulings gradually map out the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Court, while declaring that 'schools are not totalitarian enclaves,' also upheld corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion backpack searches, narrowing the boundaries of those rights.
why: Each ruling is explained in five or six minutes, covering background and key holdings—ideal for listeners who want to grasp at once the boundaries of speech, corporal punishment, and backpack searches in American public schools.
who: Parents, middle and high school teachers, and law students, as well as anyone wanting to understand the limits of government power and children's rights in American public schools.
skip: Listeners familiar with the Establishment Clause can skip the second case; if you already know the details of the earlier cases, jump to the corporal punishment and search cases after 25:40.

points.h: The Flag-Salute Case: Student Rights Enter the Schoolhouse
points.body: Can students really claim First Amendment rights during class? This case actually began with religion: Jehovah's Witnesses families believed saluting the flag violated the commandments against other gods and idolatry, so they refused to salute and pledge. In 1940 the Supreme Court ruled against them, and World War II led more districts to require daily salutes and pledges. West Virginia expelled students who refused to recite the pledge, labeled them delinquents, and fined or jailed their parents. In 1943, the Court reversed 6–3, with Justice Jackson writing on Flag Day: no official can define orthodoxy in politics, nationalism, religion, or other opinion; students need not confess words that contradict their hearts or make empty gestures. This was the first time the Court established that students have some First Amendment rights inside school.

During the Cold War, America cast itself as a 'God-fearing' nation, adding 'Under God' to the Pledge in 1954, and more public schools began reading scripture or praying before class. In 1951, New York's Board of Regents asked religious leaders to compose a short, interfaith prayer, leaving adoption to each district. The district that implemented it allowed students to opt out, but parents of ten students still sued. In 1962, Engel v. Vitale struck it down 6–1; the key was not coercion but that the prayer was government-written, itself constituting an establishment of religion. Justice Black quoted Madison: the first experiment on our liberties should raise an alarm; the same power that can establish Christianity to the exclusion of other religions can easily establish one sect of Christianity. The decision sparked fierce backlash, and the plaintiff families faced ridicule and harassment.

In December 1965, Des Moines middle and high school students planned to wear black armbands to protest U.S. involvement in Vietnam. The school announced in advance that refusal to remove them would lead to suspension; some students—including four siblings—wore them and were suspended. In 1969, the Supreme Court ruled for the students 7–2. The issue was not ordinary dress code but a quiet, passive expression akin to pure speech, and it did not disrupt class. Without evidence of actual or reasonably foreseeable material disruption of schoolwork, school officials may not suppress student opinion. The opinion declared that public schools are not totalitarian enclaves, and students and teachers do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate. This 'substantial disruption' test became the benchmark for campus speech. Justice Black dissented, predicting students would resist nearly all rules; the hosts note that this slippery-slope argument sounds quite absurd.

In 1983, Hazelwood East High School's student newspaper, The Spectrum, had two articles that unsettled Principal Reynolds: one on teenage pregnancy used pseudonyms but might still identify the interviewee, and a divorce story named and criticized a student's parent. Reynolds decided to delete the entire two pages rather than just the articles, citing lack of time to edit and the need to publish before the semester's end. In 1988, the Supreme Court ruled for the school 5–3. The key distinction was between 'tolerating student speech' and 'promoting student speech': the paper was funded by the school, readers would perceive school endorsement, and the two pieces were indeed immature in journalistic ethics. The Court held that schools may regulate content they promote. This drew the first clear boundary around Tinker's rights.

points.h: Corporal Punishment Is Not Cruel and Unusual
points.body: Host Tracy suddenly recalled that many teachers kept wooden paddles on their desks when she was young, and research showed corporal punishment has not disappeared in America. In the 1977 case Ingram v. Wright, the school's regulation paddle was less than two feet long, three to four inches wide, and half an inch thick, with one to five strokes per incident; but Ingram was hit more than 20 times in a single event and needed medical attention. The Court did not dwell on whether this particular case was excessive; it ruled that school corporal punishment does not violate the Constitution. The Eighth Amendment protects convicted persons; prisoners and schoolchildren are separated by 'the harsh fact of criminal conviction and incarceration.' Schools are open places with teachers and peers as witnesses, and students go home at the end of the day. According to NEA statistics, corporal punishment remains legal in public schools in 17 states and is actually practiced in 14; boys, Black students, and students with disabilities are paddled at significantly higher rates.

points.h: Backpack Search Needs Only Reasonable Suspicion
points.body: In 1980, a 14-year-old New Jersey student, TLO, was reported by a teacher for smoking in the restroom. Vice Principal Choplik searched her purse, found cigarettes and rolling papers, then continued searching and found what appeared to be marijuana and evidence of drug dealing. TLO was convicted and sentenced to one year of probation. In 1985, the Supreme Court upheld the search 6–3. The Court acknowledged that the Fourth Amendment applies to school officials and that students have an expectation of privacy, but it must be balanced against the school's need to maintain a learning environment. Therefore, school searches need not meet the probable cause required for police; a lower threshold of reasonable suspicion suffices. The teacher's report gave the vice principal reason to suspect she had cigarettes, and the purse was the obvious place; seeing rolling papers naturally extended suspicion to marijuana, which was also reasonable.

terms.def: The threshold established in Tinker for disciplining student speech: there must be actual material disruption or evidence that disruption would reasonably result.

In our system, state-operated schools may not be enclaves of totalitarianism. School officials do not possess absolute authority over their students. Students in school as well as out of school are persons under our Constitution. They are possessed of fundamental rights which the state must respect, just as they themselves must respect their obligations to the state.
